To be fair, I don't have anything against the Apple Vision Pro. I'm sure the Apple Vision Pro is a great product. But the iPhone Duo and the Apple Vision Pro are simply not the same thing.

There's a narrative that the iPhone Duo could suffer the same fate as the Apple Vision Pro. The reasoning is that its pricing and device-specific software might make it a critical darling but a commercial flop. But the two situations are completely different.

The iPhone Duo won't face the same biggest challenges as the Apple Vision Pro

The biggest problem with this view is that the Apple Vision Pro simply doesn't replace a core device. It can serve as a portable cinema, a better gaming display, and the mixed reality experience can genuinely be impressive.

The Apple Vision Pro doesn't replace your iPhone or iPad. It's an immersive world you can fit in a carry-on, but it's essentially a stationary-use device, not a small tablet you can slip into your pocket and take anywhere.

Then there's the price. The iPhone Duo's $1,999 starting price certainly isn't cheap, but it's better than feared. Consumers have always been willing to pay up for premium smartphones, simply because phones are so important in modern life.

The Apple Vision Pro's original $3,499 starting price was never exactly appealing, and it's now risen to $3,699—almost enough to buy two iPhone Duos, or enough to get an iPhone Quattro.

Practicality, portability, and an affordable price: these three factors combined make the biggest difference. The Apple Vision Pro couldn't become a mainstream consumer product for these reasons, and as a result, it has struggled to fully realise its potential.

The iPhone Duo combines an iPhone and a small iPad into one

The iPhone Duo combines the functionality of an iPhone and a small iPad into one device, yet it still fits in your pocket. Its pricing is roughly equivalent to buying an iPhone 16 Pro this year and upgrading to an iPhone 17 Pro next year—a pattern that isn't all that unusual.

Admittedly, the iPhone Duo will inevitably face plenty of challenges in software optimisation, particularly with third-party apps. But Apple has already built a fairly comprehensive story around its operating system and first-party apps, and developers will soon have the tools to create great applications for this versatile foldable screen.

For me, the biggest challenge for the iPhone Duo is that it doesn't yet quite manage to be a truly top-tier iPhone—hopefully future versions will get there.

The hardware itself is still quite refined, and the operating system experience is smooth. But until it can run iPad apps (an issue that's actually less complicated than some people make it out to be), it can't truly be described as an iPad when unfolded; plus, the machine costs two thousand pounds, yet the cameras are the same as the 16e. Compared to rival foldables from competitors, factoring in practicality, the value proposition of this device is genuinely poor. In whichever category it sits, it's not the best Apple device in that class.

These aren't just 'first-generation growing pains.' Apple should have surpassed Samsung, Honor, and Google across the board, but it clearly chose not to.

Ideally, you'd combine the best elements of every iPhone, including a foldable screen. But for now, the iPhone 18 Pro still has the edge in cameras and Face ID.

More importantly, for a group of consumers looking to try out a brand-new iPhone form factor, the trade-offs mentioned above aren't actually that big a sacrifice.

To put it mildly, the Apple Vision Pro certainly wishes the challenges it faced were those of the iPhone Duo.
